rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr takes Ṭuwā as a kind of valley, narrow like folded cloth or deep like a lined well; a valley outside Mecca was called Dhū Ṭuwā, where arriving pilgrims are recommended to bathe.
rows.anchor: اسم لصنف من الأودية يكون ضيقا بمنزلة الثوب المطوي أو غائرا كالبئر المطوية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He notes disagreement over whether Ṭuwā is declinable: it may be indeclinable as a foreign name or because it is altered from Ṭāw, as ʿUmar from ʿĀmir.
rows.anchor: هل ينصرف أو يمنع من الصرف بناء على أنه اسم أعجمي أو لأنه معدول عن طاو

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read Ṭuwā without tanwīn, treating it as diptote.
rows.anchor: بلا تنوين على منعه من الصرف

rows.speaker: ابن عامر وعاصم وحمزة والكسائي وخلف
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir, ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Khalaf read it with tanwīn because it is a masculine valley name.
rows.anchor: لأنه اسم واد مذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verbal predication in “I chose you” strengthens the assertion rather than restricting it; the unusual, surprising news calls for reinforcement to prevent Moses from doubting it.
rows.anchor: لأن المقام ليس مقام إفادة التخصيص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iختيار means making an effort to seek what is good; the effort form here is used for excellent pursuit of good.
rows.anchor: تكلف طلب ما هو خير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to listen to revelation follows from being chosen: the choice means selecting Moses to receive what God will reveal.
rows.anchor: وفرع على الإخبار باختياره أن أمر بالاستماع للوحي لأنه أثر الاختيار إذ لا معنى للاختيار إلا اختياره لتلقي ما سيوحي الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The immediate command concerns the revelation being delivered then; Moses' duty to listen to future revelations is understood a fortiori.
rows.anchor: ما يوحى إليه حينئذ من الكلام

rows.speaker: حمزة
rows.claim: Ḥamza alone reads “We chose you,” using the pronoun of majesty.
rows.anchor: حمزة وحده { وأنا اخترناك بضميري التعظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in “for what is revealed” strengthens the transitive link from istamiʿ to its object.
rows.anchor: للتقوية في تعدية فعل ( استمع ) إلى مفعوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the lām may depend on “I chose you,” meaning “I chose you for revelation, so listen,” with the intervening clause parenthetical.
rows.anchor: معترضا بين الفعل والمتعلق به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, istamiʿ may carry the sense of aṣghi, “listen attentively.”
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يضمن استمع معنى أصغغ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The following declaration and commands are the revelation Moses was ordered to hear; the sentence is an unrestricted apposition to “what is revealed.”
rows.anchor: فالجملة بدل من { ما يوحى }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's proper name signifies the necessary existent, worthy of every praise; knowing the name God has made His own is the first divine matter Moses must know and the basis for the revealed rulings to follow.
rows.anchor: ووقع الإخبار عن ضمير المتكلم باسمه العلم الدال على الذات الواجب الوجود المستحق لجميع المحامد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The naming also alludes to how people first introduce themselves by name: God knows His interlocutor Moses and makes His own name known to him.
rows.anchor: أن أول ما يتعارف به المتلاقون أن يعرفوا أسماءهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabic name for God is Allāh; the Torah uses YHWH or Ehyeh in Exodus 3 and 6, though its frequent terms are “Lord” or “God,” perhaps reflecting translators' wording.
rows.anchor: ( يهوه ) أو ( أهيه ) المذكور في الإصحاح الثالث من سفر الخروج في التوراة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr notes further Torah occurrences of the name in Exodus 31:18 and 32:16, while suggesting that translators may account for the wording.
rows.anchor: وقد ذكر اسم الله في مواضع من التوراة مثل الإصحاح الحادي والثلاثين من سفر الخروج في الفقرة الثامنة عشرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He observes that Ehyeh and YHWH have letters close to those of the Arabic word ilāh.
rows.anchor: قريب الحروف من كلمة إله في العربية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He reports a view that the Hebrew divine name is “لاهم,” and suggests its final mīm may underlie the tanwīn in ilāh.
rows.anchor: ولعل الميم في آخره هي أصل التنوين في إله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic particle reassures Moses, who is treated as potentially doubtful because the news is strange and might prompt doubt.
rows.anchor: نزل منزلة الشاك لأن غرابة الخبر تعرض السامع للشك فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The separating pronoun adds emphasis, not exclusivity; the point is that the speaker bears the name Allāh, an identity predication rather than a derivational one.
rows.anchor: لزيادة تقوية الخبر ، وليس بمفيد للقصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He compares the identity predication to the statement that the Messiah is God in 5:72.
rows.anchor: الذين قالوا إن الله هو المسيح ابن مريم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “There is no deity except Me” is a second predicate of inna's subject.
rows.anchor: خبر ثان عن اسم ( إن )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The declaration is intended to establish Moses' knowledge of God's oneness.
rows.anchor: والمقصود منه حصول العلم لموسى بوحدانية الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to worship follows from God's sole divinity, which entails His exclusive right to worship; worship includes words and deeds of glorification and sincerity of heart.
rows.anchor: العبادة تجمع معنى العمل الدال على التعظيم من قول وفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer is singled out because it gathers the states of worship; establishing it means maintaining it without neglect.
rows.anchor: إدامتها ، أي عدم الغفلة عنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhikr may mean mental remembrance or verbal remembrance.
rows.anchor: بمعنى التذكر بالعقل ، ويجوز أن يكون الذكر باللسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām may express purpose: pray in order to remember God, since prayer recalls the Creator through the worshipper's sense of standing before Him in intimate conversation.
rows.anchor: أي أقم الصلاة لأجل أن تذكرني ، لأن الصلاة تذكر العبد بخالقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Together with 29:45, the purpose of prayer implies piety: remembering God's commands and prohibitions leads the worshipper to obey and avoid what He forbids; Moses receives this wisdom generally, while Muhammad receives it in detail.
rows.anchor: يظهر أن التقوى من حكمة مشروعية الصلاة لأن المكلف إذا ذكر أمر الله ونهيه فعل ما أمره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the lām marks time: establish prayer at the time appointed for God's remembrance.
rows.anchor: للتوقيت ، أي أقم الصلاة عند الوقت الذي جعلته لذكري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On another reading, verbal remembrance moves the heart, includes praise and acknowledgment of God's right, and points to the wisdom in prayer times; the context supplies an ellipsis.
rows.anchor: لأن ذكر اللسان يحرك ذكر القلب ويشتمل على الثناء على الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement begins a second fundamental teaching after monotheism: affirmation of requital; “the Hour” conventionally names the Resurrection or reckoning.
rows.anchor: مستأنفة لابتداء إعلام بأصل ثان من أصول الدين بعد أصل التوحيد ، وهو إثبات الجزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause “I nearly conceal it” may be circumstantial to “the Hour” or parenthetical between the main statement and its rationale.
rows.anchor: في موضع الحال من الساعة ، أو معترضة بين جملة وعلتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Concealment means covering or not showing; here it metaphorically means not disclosing the Hour's time.
rows.anchor: الستر وعدم الإظهار ، وأريد به هنا المجاز عن عدم الإعلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In common usage kāda indicates that the reported act is near to occurring, while the act itself remains unfulfilled; 72:19 illustrates this.
rows.anchor: تدل على مقاربة وقوع الفعل المخبر به عنها ، فالفعل بعدها في حيز الانتفاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the Hour's timing is already hidden, the wording “I nearly conceal it” is unclear, prompting several interpretations, of which Ibn ʿĀshūr identifies three as strongest.
rows.anchor: مخفية الوقت ، كان قوله { أكاد أخفيها } غير واضح المقصود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation is that God conceals mention of the Hour, leaving its time unspoken; repeated mention in the Qur'an only made its deniers more obstinate.
rows.anchor: الحديث عنها ، أي من شدة إرادة إخفاء وقتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation treats kāda as extra emphasis: God does conceal the Hour, which therefore arrives only suddenly.
rows.anchor: زائدة هنا بمنزلة زيادة كان في بعض المواضع تأكيدا للإخفاء

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī reads akhfīhā as “make it manifest,” taking the hamza as privative, like removing a covering; the Hour's occurrence is near.
rows.anchor: وتأول أبو علي الفارسي معنى { أخفيها } بمعنى أظهرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is an unusual use of kāda, to be compared with the negative construction “they almost did not do it” in 2:71.
rows.anchor: غرائب استعمال ( كاد ) فيضم إلى استعمال نفيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The purpose phrase “so every soul may be repaid” attaches to “is coming”; the intervening words are parenthetical.
rows.anchor: واللام في { لتجزى كل نفس } متعلق بآتية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse teaches the wisdom of establishing a day of requital.
rows.anchor: وهذا تعليم بحكمة جعل يوم للجزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “For what it strives for” means for what each soul does; applying striving to deeds is a metonym, as at 17:19.
rows.anchor: بما تعمل ، فإطلاق السعي على العمل مجاز مرسل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the Hour is coming though its time is hidden, Moses is warned against deniers who exploit its delayed appearance to dissuade him from belief; this follows especially from “I nearly conceal it.”
rows.anchor: الإيمان بها قوم لا يؤمنون بوقوعها اغترارا بتأخر ظهورها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He links the deniers' appeal to delay with 17:51 and their later denial of certainty with 45:32.
rows.anchor: وعد الله حق والساعة لا ريب فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition is phrased as telling an unbeliever not to turn Moses away, intensifying the command that Moses avoid even slight accommodation of the denier; it forbids the cause by naming its result.
rows.anchor: صيغة نهي من لا يؤمن بالساعة عن أن يصد موسى عن الإيمان بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses must not be pliant toward a person who turns him away or heed him, lest that lenience embolden the person; the wording resembles “do not let me find you doing this.”
rows.anchor: أي لا تكن لين الشكيمة لمن يصدك ولا تصغ إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr compares the construction to the idiom “Do not let me know you doing this” and “Do not let me see you here.”
rows.anchor: لا أعرفنك تفعل كذا ولا أرينك ههنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase signals why unbelievers dissuade Moses: they follow desire without evidence, whereas evidence supports belief in the Hour through the rationale in 20:15.
rows.anchor: للإيماء بالصلة إلى تعليل الصد ، أي لا داعي لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “You would perish” means you would be ruined; ruin figuratively denotes the worst condition, as in 9:42.
rows.anchor: أي هلك . والهلاك مستعار لأسوأ الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ruin is linked to committing the prohibited act, not grammatically to the prohibition itself; hence the fa is not jussive, since a conditional particle cannot replace the result after lā here.
rows.anchor: لا على النهي ، ولذلك جيء بالتفريع بالفاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address reasons through each command and prohibition: identify God and His oneness, derive worship and prayer, affirm the Hour and its requital, warn against deniers, and show that violating the warning brings ruin.
rows.anchor: فابتدىء بالإعلام بأن الذي يكلمه هو الله ، وأنه لا إله إلا هو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sharing the mission with Aaron multiplies the call and also spurs Aaron to preach; their messages glorify God, teach His attributes and commandments, and bring the people into faith and piety, multiplying remembrance through proclamation.
rows.anchor: تشريكه في الدعوة ولم يكن لأخيه من قبل ، وذلك يجعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr connects the benefits Moses requested with the command not to slacken in remembrance: delivering God's commands and prohibitions increases their glorification and remembrance.
rows.anchor: لا تضعفا في تبليغ الرسالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Cooperation in the mission lets the brothers divide the work needed for daily life, reducing time spent on necessities and freeing more time for preaching.
rows.anchor: تقليل من الاشتغال بضرورات الحياة ، إذ يمكن أن يقتسما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses knew Pharaoh's severity and tyranny would obstruct the people from leaving misguidance, and that preaching would expose its callers to trial; he sought help to overcome that trial and devote themselves to remembrance.
rows.anchor: علمه بشدة فرعون وطغيانه ومنعه الأمة من مفارقة ضلالهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “You have always seen us” justifies Moses' requests: God knows both brothers' condition and need, and Moses entrusts their best interests to Him while asking according to his own knowledge.
rows.anchor: تعليل لسؤاله شرح صدره وما بعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement recalls the first creation as evidence that resurrection after death is possible; the discussion of the earth and its benefits naturally leads to the human origin and fate connected with it.
rows.anchor: فإن ذكر خلق الأرض ومنافعها يستدعي إكمال ذكر المهم للناس من أحوالها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human creation from earth resembles plants growing from it, and resurrection resembles plants emerging; 71:17–18 makes the comparison explicit.
rows.anchor: فكان خلق أصل الإنسان من الأرض شبيها بخروج النبات منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fronting “from it” first emphasizes earth as the origin of both creations; fronting “in it” in the middle pairs it with the other two phrases.
rows.anchor: فأما المجرور الأول والمجرور الثالث فللاهتمام بكون الأرض مبدأ الخلق الأول والخلق الثاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse makes burial in earth the prescribed way to dispose of the dead, whether trench or niche; burning, drowning, or aboveground coffins contradict divine custom and human nature, which call for covering the fallen body in earth.
rows.anchor: على أن دفن الأموات في الأرض هو الطريقة الشرعية لمواراة الموتى سواء كان شقا في الأرض أو لحدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He links the first human burial to Cain and Abel: God sent a crow to show the killer how to cover his brother, and divine laws then required burial in earth, as recounted in 5:31.
rows.anchor: وكذلك كانت أول مواراة في البشر حين قتل أحد ابني آدم أخاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tārah means one time or occasion, and its plural is tārāt.
rows.anchor: والتارة : المرة ، وجمعها تارات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn al-Aʿrābī says the alif in tārah originates in hamza, which common use dropped; some point to the hamza in the plural form taʾr as evidence.
rows.anchor: الأعرابي : أصل ألفها همزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr considers tārah an underived, frozen noun.
rows.anchor: ويظهر أنها اسم جامد ليس له أصل مشتق منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emergence is resurrection after the bodies have been recreated inside the earth; calling it another time points to re-creation as in the first creation, as stated at 21:104.
rows.anchor: هو إخراجها إلى الحشر بعد إعادة هياكل الأجسام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's departure and collection of resources show that he promptly prepared for the appointed contest instead of wasting time.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى أن فرعون بادر بالاستعداد لهذا الموعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tawallā means to depart literally; Pharaoh left to send messengers to the cities to gather people known for magic, as in 79:22–23.
rows.anchor: وهو هنا مستعمل في حقيقته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The departure and gathering are compared with Pharaoh's turning away and summoning in 79:22–23.
rows.anchor: ثم أدبر يسعى فحشر فنادى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gathering his scheme means planning how to debate Moses, arrange for the magicians to appear victorious, and persuade onlookers that Moses has no truth.
rows.anchor: تدبير أسلوب مناظرة موسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This old debating tactic uses every form of confusion, disparagement, and smear to weaken an opponent and unsettle his judgment.
rows.anchor: وهذا أسلوب قديم في المناظرات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here jamʿ means preparing and fully arranging an opinion or plan, as in the command to make a plan in 10:71.
rows.anchor: فالجمع هنا مستعمل في معنى إعداد الرأي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, he gathered the people of his scheme, meaning the magicians, as in 26:38.
rows.anchor: فجمع أهل كيده ، أي جمع السحرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kayd is concealing intended harm until the time it is carried out; compare 7:183.
rows.anchor: إخفاء ما به الضر إلى وقت فعله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Then Pharaoh came to the appointment; thumma marks both real time passing during preparation and the greater importance of appearing to display its result.
rows.anchor: وثم للمهلة الحقيقية والرتبية معا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Moses said to them” begins an explanatory sentence: Pharaoh's arrival naturally raises the question of what happened next, and Moses opens by admonishing the magicians.
rows.anchor: مستأنفة استئنافا بيانيا ، لأن قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Them” may refer to the magicians implied by the promised matching magic, or to everyone present, since Pharaoh and his court could see and hear; the latter is implied by the gathered men of Pharaoh's scheme.
rows.anchor: عائد إلى معلوم من قوله { فلنأتينك بسحر مثله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If “woe to you” is a genuine imprecation, Moses may be addressing only the magicians, not Pharaoh, so he does not violate the command to speak gently to Pharaoh.
rows.anchor: يجوز أن يكون أراد به حقيقة الدعاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, after seeing that gentleness did not soften Pharaoh's settled disbelief, Moses may have been specially permitted to speak harshly, restricting the general command of gentleness, as Muhammad was permitted to fight in 22:39.
rows.anchor: أغلظ القول زجرا له بأمر خاص من الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, seeing the magicians mislead the crowd by invoking Pharaoh's might as proof of divine support, Moses regarded forceful verbal repudiation as the fitting way to oppose wrong.
rows.anchor: رأى واجبا عليه تغيير المنكر بلسانه بأقصى ما يستطيع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word may instead express astonishment at a strange state, meaning “I marvel at you and warn you”; the Prophet used a similar expression to Abū Baṣīr.
rows.anchor: مستعملة في التعجب من حال غريبة

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet called Abū Baṣīr “a fire-stirrer of war,” an expression Ibn ʿĀshūr cites as an example of astonished exclamation; no grading is given.
rows.anchor: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم لأبي بصير : ( ويل أمه مسعر حرب )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wayl names punishment or evil and has no verb.
rows.anchor: اسم للعذاب والشر ، وليس له فعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Waylakum” may be accusative with an omitted warning or exhortation verb, or with an omitted vocative particle, as in “O woe to us”; see 2:79.
rows.anchor: على إضمار فعل على التحذير أو الإغراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iftirāʾ means fabricating a lie; combining it with “a lie” adds emphasis, as at 5:103.
rows.anchor: اختلاق الكذب . والجمع بينه وبين كذبا } للتأكيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses calls their sorcery a fabrication: they make ropes seem like snakes, claim divine backing, call Moses a liar and magician, or deify Pharaoh and his gods; their blasphemous claims varied.
rows.anchor: والافتراء الذي عناه موسى هو ما يخيلونه للناس من الشعوذة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning against attributing lies to God is reinforced by 5:103, which describes disbelievers inventing falsehood about God.
rows.anchor: يفترون على الله الكذب في سورة المائدة

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read yashaṭkum with fatḥa on yāʾ, from saḥata, “uproot”; this is the Hijazi dialect.
rows.anchor: مضارع سحته : إذا استأصله

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي وحفص عن عاصم وخلف ورويس عن يعقوب
rows.claim: Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim, Khalaf, and Ruways from Yaʿqūb read yusḥitkum with ḍamma on yāʾ, from asḥata, the Najdi and Tamimi dialect; both readings are eloquent.
rows.anchor: حمزة ، والكسائي ، وحفص عن عاصم ، وخلف ، ورويس عن يعقوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Whoever fabricates has failed” is circumstantial to the prohibition and supplies its rationale: earlier fabricators failed to achieve their aim.
rows.anchor: في موضع الحال من ضمير { لا تفتروا }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative pronoun man is general: whoever fabricates.
rows.anchor: و { من } الموصولة للعموم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The argument functions as the major premise of a categorical syllogism.
rows.anchor: وموقع هذه الجملة بعد التي قبلها كموقع القضية الكبرى من القياس الاقتراني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses signals that he would not falsely claim revelation: knowing that God would destroy him and that fabricators fail, he would not undertake such a lie.
rows.anchor: وفي كلام موسى إعلان بأنه لا يتقول على الله ما لم يأمره به لأنه يعلم أنه يستأصله بعذاب ويعلم خيبة من افترى على الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' admonition led to disagreement: it affected some, while others feared losing resolve, so they consulted one another about what to do.
rows.anchor: وهذا يؤذن بأن منهم من تركت فيه الموعظة بعض الأثر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tanāzuʿ is reciprocal pulling, like drawing from a well or tugging a garment; figuratively it is disagreement as each person tries to persuade others of his view.
rows.anchor: تفاعل من النزع ، وهو الجذب من البئر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Najwā is secret conversation; they withdrew to speak privately and decide without outsiders learning their plan.
rows.anchor: الحديث السري ، أي اختلوا وتحادثوا سرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Making najwā the object of asarrū intensifies concealment, like saying “they hid their secret” or “a poet composed poetry.”
rows.anchor: يفيد المبالغة في الكتمان ، كأنه قيل : أسروا سرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The speakers may have witnessed Moses' display at Pharaoh's court or learned of it through widespread report.
rows.anchor: قد يكون بعضهم ممن شاهد ما أتى به موسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “you” are the elite addressed by the magicians; their accusation echoes 20:57, with a further possibility that the magicians privately feared Moses and Aaron would monopolize magic and render them irrelevant.
rows.anchor: ووجه اتهامهما بذلك هو ما تقدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The charge echoes Pharaoh's earlier question to Moses in 20:57.
rows.anchor: أجئتنا لتخرجنا من أرضنا بسحرك يا موسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭarīqah means a customary way or practice, likened to a road that a traveler follows; al-muthlā is the feminine of al-amthal, derived from good condition or excellence.
rows.anchor: شبهت بالطريق الذي يسير فيه السائر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-amthal describes the person closest to good and best in condition among his people.
rows.anchor: أي أقربهم إلى الخير وأحسنهم حالا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The magicians appeal to group zeal for ancestral custom and morality, then urge their audience to gather every stratagem and resource to defeat Moses.
rows.anchor: غيرة على عوائدهم ، فإن لكل أمة غيرة على عوائدها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bāʾ in “take away your way” makes yadhhabā transitive; it means to take it away and binds the verb to its object more strongly than a direct object, as at 2:17.
rows.anchor: والباء في { بطريقتكم } لتعدية فعل

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read fa-ajmiʿū with hamzat al-qaṭʿ and kasra on mīm, from ajmaʿa amrahu: make the plan agreed and settled.
rows.anchor: بهمزة قطع وكسر الميم أمرا من : أجمع أمره

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr reads fa-jmaʿū with hamzat al-waṣl and fatḥa on mīm, from jamaʿa: gather, unite, and cooperate; this counters their earlier disagreement.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو { فاجمعوا } بهمزة وصل وبفتح الميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Abū ʿAmr's reading, gathering suggests cooperation, figuratively collecting divergent views and answering the earlier “they disputed their plan.”
rows.anchor: أطلق الجمع على التعاضد والتعاون ، تشبيها للشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their act is called a scheme because they agreed to convince the public that Moses' sign was ordinary by matching or exceeding it, diverting people and erasing its distinctive force.
rows.anchor: لأنهم تواطئوا على أن يظهروا للعامة أن ما جاء به موسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The magicians' scheme arose because people had heard Moses' call and miracle and were perplexed; 26:38–40 describes their assembly and the public being urged to attend.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن عامة الناس تسامعوا بدعوة موسى
